questions.stem: The wound care nurse is reviewing five pressure injuries on residents of a long-term care unit. For each description, select the stage.

Shallow open area with a pink-red wound bed and no slough
Full-thickness loss with visible fat but no bone or tendon
Full-thickness loss with exposed bone at the heel
Wound bed covered by black eschar so the depth cannot be seen

options.text: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4
Unstageable
Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3

Unstageable
Stage 1

Unstageable

rationale.correct: Stage pressure injuries by the deepest tissue visible; slough or eschar that hides the base makes the injury unstageable.

perOption.b1:a: Intact skin with non-blanchable redness is stage 1.
perOption.b1:b: This description fits stage 1, not stage 2.
perOption.b1:c: This description fits stage 1, not stage 3.
perOption.b1:d: This description fits stage 1, not stage 4.
perOption.b1:e: This description fits stage 1, not unstageable.
perOption.b2:a: This description fits stage 2, not stage 1.
perOption.b2:b: Partial-thickness loss with a pink-red bed is stage 2.
perOption.b2:c: This description fits stage 2, not stage 3.
perOption.b2:d: This description fits stage 2, not stage 4.
perOption.b2:e: This description fits stage 2, not unstageable.
perOption.b3:a: This description fits stage 3, not stage 1.
perOption.b3:b: This description fits stage 3, not stage 2.
perOption.b3:c: Full-thickness skin loss with visible fat is stage 3.
perOption.b3:d: This description fits stage 3, not stage 4.
perOption.b3:e: This description fits stage 3, not unstageable.
perOption.b4:a: This description fits stage 4, not stage 1.
perOption.b4:b: This description fits stage 4, not stage 2.
perOption.b4:c: This description fits stage 4, not stage 3.
perOption.b4:d: Exposed bone, tendon or muscle is stage 4.
perOption.b4:e: This description fits stage 4, not unstageable.
perOption.b5:a: This description fits unstageable, not stage 1.
perOption.b5:b: This description fits unstageable, not stage 2.
perOption.b5:c: This description fits unstageable, not stage 3.
perOption.b5:d: This description fits unstageable, not stage 4.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing Braden scale scores for four residents on admission to a long-term care unit. Which resident has the highest risk for a pressure injury?

options.text: A resident who is bedbound and incontinent, with a score of 9
A resident who walks with a walker, with a score of 15
A resident who is independent and continent, with a score of 19
A resident who is fully mobile and eats well, with a score of 23

rationale.correct: Braden scale: 6 to 23 points; a lower score means a higher risk.

perOption.a: Lower Braden scores mean higher risk; 9 or below is very high risk.
perOption.b: A score of 15 to 18 is mild risk.
perOption.c: A score of 19 or above is no significant risk.
perOption.d: 23 is the highest possible score and the lowest risk.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old client on bed rest after a stroke has a reddened sacrum that blanches and a poor appetite. Which interventions help prevent pressure injuries? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reposition the client at least every 2 hours
Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or lower
Float the heels off the bed on pillows
Offer protein-rich snacks and supplements
Massage the reddened sacrum to improve flow
Sit the client on a donut-shaped cushion

rationale.correct: Prevention: reposition, reduce shear, use support surfaces, manage moisture and nutrition; no massage or donuts.

perOption.a: This relieves pressure.
perOption.b: This reduces shear on the sacrum, unless contraindicated.
perOption.e: Massage can damage the tissue further.
perOption.f: Donuts reduce blood flow to the surrounding tissue.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Five days after an open bowel resection, an obese client with diabetes coughs hard and says, "Something just gave way." The nurse finds loops of bowel protruding through the incision. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Cover the bowel with sterile saline-moistened gauze
Gently push the bowel back inside and apply a binder
Apply a thick dry dressing over the bowel and tape it securely
Help the client sit up straight to splint the abdomen

rationale.correct: Evisceration: cover with saline-moistened sterile dressings, place in low Fowler's with knees bent, stay with the client and notify the surgeon.

perOption.a: This protects the organs and keeps them moist.
perOption.b: This risks injury and contamination.
perOption.c: Dry gauze sticks to and damages tissue.
perOption.d: Sitting upright raises abdominal pressure; low Fowler's with bent knees is used.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the second day after an abdominal hysterectomy, the nurse notes thin, watery, pale pink drainage on the dressing, about the size of a coin. The client is afebrile, and the incision edges are closed. How should the nurse document the drainage?

options.text: Serosanguineous
Purulent
Sanguineous
Serous

rationale.correct: Serous = clear; sanguineous = bloody; serosanguineous = pink and watery; purulent = pus.

perOption.a: Serosanguineous drainage is a thin mix of serum and blood.
perOption.b: Purulent drainage is thick and yellow, green or tan.
perOption.c: Sanguineous drainage is bright red blood.
perOption.d: Serous drainage is clear and straw-colored.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with a stage 3 sacral pressure injury has an albumin of 2.8 g/dL and eats about half of each meal. Which nutrients are most important to promote wound healing?

options.text: Protein, vitamin C and zinc
Sodium and potassium
Caffeine and simple sugars
A very low-fat, low-calorie diet

rationale.correct: Wound healing needs protein, calories, vitamin C, zinc and fluids.

perOption.a: These support collagen synthesis and tissue repair.
perOption.b: These are not central to healing.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's leg ulcer has new redness and odor, and the provider prescribes a wound culture. The old dressing is soaked with drainage. How should the nurse obtain the culture?

options.text: Clean the wound with sterile saline, then swab viable tissue
Swab the drainage on the old dressing before throwing it away
Swab the black eschar at the center of the wound
Apply povidone-iodine, then swab the wound right away

rationale.correct: Wound culture: clean with saline, then swab clean, viable tissue using the Levine technique.

perOption.a: Cleaning removes surface contaminants so the culture reflects the infection.
perOption.b: This collects contaminants.
perOption.c: Eschar is not a reliable sample.
perOption.d: Antiseptic kills the organisms being cultured.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An adult was burned when a gas grill exploded. Using the rule of nines, the nurse estimates partial- and full-thickness burns to the entire front of the trunk, the entire left arm and the front of the right leg. The face has only redness. What is the total body surface area burned, in percent?

rationale.correct: Front of trunk = 18%. Entire left arm = 9%. Front of right leg = 9%. Total = 18 + 9 + 9 = 36%. Superficial (first-degree) burns such as redness alone are not counted.
references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Estimate burn size with the rule of nines.

questions.stem: A client rescued from a house fire 20 minutes ago is alert and talking. The client has blisters on both forearms and pain rated 8 out of 10. Which finding is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Singed nasal hair, soot around the mouth and a hoarse voice
Large, intact blisters across both forearms and the backs of the hands
Pain rated 8 out of 10 in the burned areas
Anxiety about family members still in hospital

rationale.correct: Inhalation injury threatens the airway; prepare for early intubation before swelling worsens.

perOption.a: These suggest inhalation injury; airway swelling can progress quickly to obstruction.
perOption.b: Blisters need care but are not an airway threat.
perOption.c: Pain is treated after the airway is assessed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 80 kg adult was burned at 1400 and has partial- and full-thickness burns over 36% of the body. The client has no other injuries and arrived at 1430, and the burn team uses the Parkland formula (4 mL × kg × %TBSA). How many mL of lactated Ringer's should the client receive in the first 8 hours after the burn?

rationale.correct: Total 24-hour volume = 4 × 80 × 36 = 11,520 mL. Half is given in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn = 5,760 mL.
references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate burn fluid resuscitation with the Parkland formula.

questions.stem: A 70 kg adult with major burns is receiving lactated Ringer's by the Parkland formula. Which finding best shows that fluid resuscitation is adequate?

options.text: Urine output of about 35 to 50 mL/hr
Urine output of 10 mL/hr for 2 hours
Blood pressure of 180/100 mm Hg
A weight loss of 2 kg since admission

rationale.correct: Titrate burn fluids to urine output (0.5 mL/kg/hr for adults; higher for electrical injury).

perOption.a: Urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/hr is the main guide for titrating burn fluids.
perOption.b: This means under-resuscitation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Twelve hours after a major flame burn, a client is receiving IV fluids by the Parkland formula and has a urine output of 40 mL/hr. Which pattern of laboratory results should the nurse expect at this point?

options.text: A high potassium and a high hematocrit
A low potassium and a low hematocrit
A high albumin and a high total protein
A low sodium with no other changes

rationale.correct: Emergent phase: hyperkalemia, hemoconcentration and metabolic acidosis.

perOption.a: Cell damage releases potassium, and plasma loss concentrates the blood.
perOption.b: These are more typical later, during fluid mobilization.
perOption.c: Albumin falls as it leaks out of the vessels.
perOption.d: This is not the main pattern.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Predict lab changes in the emergent burn phase.

questions.stem: A client has full-thickness burns all the way around the right lower leg. Six hours after admission, which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: A weakening pedal pulse and new numbness in the foot
A dry, leathery, white appearance of the burned skin
Little pain over the center of the burned area
Mild swelling of the toes on the burned leg

rationale.correct: Burns that circle a limb need frequent neurovascular checks and may need an escharotomy.

perOption.a: Tight eschar can cut off circulation; an escharotomy may be needed.
perOption.b: This is expected with full-thickness burns.
perOption.c: Nerve endings are destroyed in full-thickness burns.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with burns over 40% of the body 4 hours ago has severe pain and a blood pressure of 96/58. The heart rate is 118/min, and IV fluids are running. Morphine is prescribed by several routes. By which route should the nurse give it?

options.text: IV
IM
Oral
Subcutaneous

rationale.correct: Give burn pain medication IV in the acute phase.

perOption.a: Poor perfusion makes IM and subcutaneous absorption unreliable in the emergent phase.
perOption.b: Absorption is erratic.
perOption.c: The GI tract may be slowed by ileus.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose the route for burn analgesia.

questions.stem: A client with partial-thickness burns over 25% of the body is treated with silver sulfadiazine cream twice a day and has no known drug allergies. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor?

options.text: White blood cell count
Fasting blood glucose
Thyroid hormone levels
Serum lipase

rationale.correct: Silver sulfadiazine: watch for leukopenia, and check for a sulfa allergy first.

perOption.a: Silver sulfadiazine can cause a transient leukopenia.
perOption.b: This is not the key concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old client with burns over 45% of the body is in the acute phase and has lost 4 kg in a week. Which nutrition plan supports healing?

options.text: High-calorie, high-protein feeding, often started early by tube
A low-calorie diet to reduce the workload on the kidneys and heart
A low-protein diet to limit the risk of fluid retention
Clear liquids only until the wounds have closed

rationale.correct: Burns cause hypermetabolism; meet needs with high calories and protein, often by early enteral feeding.

perOption.a: Burns greatly increase metabolic needs.
perOption.b: This slows healing.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with deep partial-thickness burns over both elbows and knees prefers to lie curled up because it hurts less. Which intervention helps prevent contractures?

options.text: Position the joints straight and use splints as prescribed
Let the client stay in the curled-up position, which is most comfortable
Avoid range-of-motion exercises until the burns heal
Place pillows under the knees to ease the pain

rationale.correct: Burn rehabilitation: positioning in extension, splints and range-of-motion exercises, with pain relief beforehand.

perOption.a: This keeps tissue from shortening during healing.
perOption.b: Flexion promotes contractures.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An electrician who touched a high-voltage line has small burns on the right hand and left foot and is alert. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Continuous cardiac monitoring
Dressing the small burns on the hand and foot
Teaching about burn care at home
Applying ice to the entry and exit wounds

rationale.correct: Electrical burns: cardiac monitoring and watching for myoglobinuria, with higher urine output goals.

perOption.a: Electrical current can cause dysrhythmias, and the visible wounds underestimate internal damage.
perOption.b: The small wounds hide deeper damage.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care for an electrical burn.

questions.stem: A worker in a factory splashes a strong alkaline liquid on the forearm and soaks the shirtsleeve. The occupational health nurse arrives. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Remove the wet sleeve and flush the arm with lots of water
Apply a weak acid to the skin to neutralize the alkali quickly
Cover the arm with a dry sterile dressing for transport
Apply burn ointment to soothe the skin

rationale.correct: Chemical burns: remove contaminated clothing (brush off dry powders first) and irrigate with large amounts of water for at least 20 minutes.

perOption.a: Removing soaked clothing and flushing stop the burning process.
perOption.b: Neutralizing can cause a heat reaction and more injury.
perOption.c: The chemical keeps burning under the dressing.
perOption.d: This traps the chemical against the skin.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old client with diabetes is admitted with cellulitis of the right lower leg and started on IV cefazolin. Which action helps the team track whether the infection is spreading?

options.text: Mark the edge of the redness on the skin and note the time
Massage the area so that the antibiotic reaches the tissue better
Keep an ice pack on the leg continuously
Keep the leg hanging down over the side of the bed

rationale.correct: Cellulitis: mark the borders, elevate the limb, give antibiotics and watch for systemic signs.

perOption.a: This shows whether the redness is spreading or shrinking.
perOption.b: This may spread the infection.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: During a skin check, a 48-year-old client with fair skin points out four spots on the back. Which spot should the nurse advise the client to have examined by a provider soon?

options.text: A mole with uneven borders and several shades that has grown
A small, round, evenly brown mole that has not changed in years
A cluster of freckles that fade every winter
A soft skin tag on the side of the neck

rationale.correct: ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border, Color, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolving.

perOption.a: Asymmetry, irregular borders, varied color and change suggest melanoma (ABCDE).
perOption.b: This is a typical benign mole.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old lifeguard asks how to lower the risk of skin cancer. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Use SPF 30 or higher and reapply every 2 hours
Get a base tan in a tanning bed before summer
Use sunscreen on cloudy days rather than sunny ones
Apply sunscreen once in the morning before work

rationale.correct: Sun safety: broad-spectrum sunscreen, reapplication, protective clothing, shade and no tanning beds.

perOption.a: Broad-spectrum sunscreen reapplied regularly reduces UV damage.
perOption.b: Tanning beds raise cancer risk.
perOption.c: UV exposure happens on all days.
perOption.d: It is reapplied every 2 hours and after swimming.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman is starting isotretinoin for severe nodular acne. Which teaching is most important?

options.text: Use two forms of birth control; the drug causes birth defects
Expect the acne to clear up completely within the first few days
Take a vitamin A supplement to support the skin
Donate blood often during treatment to stay healthy

rationale.correct: Isotretinoin: teratogenic, mood changes, dry skin and lips, no vitamin A and no blood donation.

perOption.a: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic; programs require pregnancy prevention and testing.
perOption.b: Improvement takes weeks to months.
perOption.d: Blood donation is not allowed during treatment.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old client on long-term steroids has thin, fragile skin with bruises on both forearms. Which action helps prevent skin tears?

options.text: Use a lift sheet and avoid strong tape
Pull the client up in bed by the arms
Secure dressings with strong adhesive tape
Bathe the client in hot water twice a day

rationale.correct: Skin tear prevention: lift sheets, padding, gentle handling, moisturizers and silicone tape.

perOption.a: Fragile skin tears with friction and adhesive removal.
perOption.b: Friction and pulling cause tears.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent skin tears in older adults.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the wound assessment of a client 4 days after an open hernia repair. Highlight the findings that suggest a wound infection.

cells: Thick, yellow-green, with a foul odor
Redness extending 3 cm beyond the incision

rationale.correct: Signs of wound infection: purulent drainage, spreading erythema, warmth, increasing pain and fever.

perOption.r3: Fever several days after surgery suggests wound infection.
perOption.r4: Granulation tissue is a sign of healing.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
